Good morning. I really appreciate the opportunity to be here this morning. It's rare that I have the ability to speak in a venue like this, typically conversations and questions happen informally and so to be here is certainly an honor for me.
And within the realm of community safety and community safety approaches, which is really the I think the catalyst for conversation and what might spur on questions.

However, I want to just talk a little bit about our approaches currently to community safety, some of the things we're experiencing and again just scratch the surface on that and allow an opportunity for any questions you may have.

So in 2022 I'll start with just kind of our general deployment, which I think creates some confusion and uncertainty. So our general deployment in 2022 we did a significant reorganization at Saskatoon police service.

We had embraced a traditional ComSTAT model for many years ComSTAT standing for computer statistics and in 2022 we moved away from that model and we reorganized our deployment into a district model of police officer deployment throughout the city and I'm referring specifically to our front line call for service kind of police deployment.
So moving from our ComSTAT model with divisions which were very large and very hard to manage we've moved to a district model. Now the district model was created using a very analytical approach.

We looked at the city of Saskatoon we looked at call volume by number we looked at call severity and we looked at how we could work in geographical barriers like the river like railroad tracks and we looked at the equitable distribution of work across our staff.
And so a system of deployment was developed using districts and from its onset this district model was built for growth.
We knew right away that the district model that was presented utilizing the analysis that was provided to us.
We required a certain number of police officers to fully realize the benefits of this model and we have not gotten to the point where we can fully staff our districts.
However, we have a solid growth model in place and our foundational philosophy of a district model is that the smaller geographical footprint of each district allows for a consistent police presence.
And it creates a philosophy which is which I'm passionate about where every police officer knows their community and every community knows their police officer. I believe that's so important.
So with regard to staffing in terms of our community safety approach and our capacity to fill our districts and to engage in some of that proactive policing that we really desire to do.
In previous presentations we've spoken about our current staffing. We've talked about it within the context of police population.

And we've seen a decreasing ratio over the last several years. However, our growth plan supported by the Board of Police Commissioners and supported by Council through our budget is solid and our current roadblock to realizing that plan is training.

We've been given a very strong assurance from the Saskatchewan police college that that training barrier will be substantially removed in 2026 and we're so grateful for their commitment to ensuring that we have the ability to fill seats in college and build out our growth plan as it is in our in our plan.

And so in terms of demand, what are we facing right now as a service? We have a city that's growing far and beyond any projections that I think would have been made at certain points in time, which is so encouraging and so exciting to be part of.

By growing city and the growing number of people within Saskatchewan has created a pressure on our service where in 2024 we received just under 160,000 calls for service. These are community members calling the Saskatchewan police service asking for assistance of one type or another.
In 2025 we're currently on a trajectory that would if maintained realize a call volume of 175,000 calls for service by the end of this year.
One of the main drivers of our increase in calls for service has been social disorder and we've spoken about that before in several venues.
Social disorder being those things that may not be crime, they may be crime, they may be petty crime, they may not even be crime, but there are things that cause concern for the city.

Because fear in the residents and business people and certainly can create a roadblock to effectively engaging in business where your business is operating in proximity to places where social disorder is more prominent or more often seen.

And so within that context what's our response. One of the things that I am passionate about and have asked our leadership team to reinforce throughout our organization is either the return or the establishment or the, I guess the instilling of a balanced approach.
That's what I'm really passionate about. I think in many ways or in many respects we have lost some of the balance when it comes to how we interact with people.
And I guess the simplest way to say it is our responsibility is to see every person in crisis as a community member who needs help.

And our responsibility is to ensure their safety, ensure their care in whatever context or in whatever way that is required. However, within that we also need to ensure that we are holding people accountable for behavior that would diminish quality of life.
That would affect business viability and that would instill a sense of fear or victimization in the residents of Saskatoon.

And so that philosophy I believe is permeating throughout our frontline policing staff and again it's a balance to make sure we're caring for people, but holding them accountable for their behavior in our community.

We have expanded our ARO presence. We've received so much positive feedback as an organization for our alternative response officer program and we have expanded that we have an authorized strength of 15.

We currently have 19, four of those members are in training right now, but by the well very shortly we'll have a full complement of 19 alternative response officers. One of the problems is the success of the program has led to a circumstance where they are utilized as kind of like a farm team.
For our fully trained sworn police staffing.
And the Saskatchewan police college is very grateful that we're sending AROs to their program because they're very experienced by the time they get there.
But it creates an ebb and a flow in our ARO presence. That is felt by the community and I receive telephone calls and emails from members of the community saying, hey, what happened?
I'm not seeing the AROs like I used to. And there's usually almost always a really logical explanation for that communication.
I have a strong mandate to be in communication with community, with business people. I have a desire to sustain.

To build and sustain as much of that communication personally as I can, but I'm certainly trying to instill that within our frontline policing staff right from the ARO level all the way through to our most seasoned and experienced members.
I believe communication is so very important to understand what is needed in the community, what the changes are and how we can address things in a very specific way based on specific need.
And collaboration, I can say with confidence that our relationship right now with the Saskatchewan fire department and the city of Saskatchewan is strong perhaps arguably stronger than ever before.
This concerted effort creating a cohesive team has also expanded into the creation and sustaining of excellent partnerships with community based organizations, non-government organizations,
system partners across the board. And in many ways we're pulling in the same direction, which is so very encouraging to me.
And it helps us understand what contributions we each have to some very, very complex issues.
Just a few insights that I would provide to you before opening the floor for questions.

I believe remaining connected to our frontline staff is incredibly important, so much so that I put on a bulletproof fast and I jump in a patrol car and I periodically go work a night shift with our staff.
I've done that four times this summer and it provides me with a connection to our staff, a real time view of what they're experiencing and how I can lead them better.
And that commitment has really led me to experience Saskatchewan at 2 o'clock in the morning in a fresh way.
What I see in Saskatchewan is an increasing volume of people in crisis.

People living on the streets to a clock in the morning and downtown Saskatchewan, there's a large volume of people who are predominantly homeless who are in crisis who are experiencing challenges I will never know.
I will never know in my life at least I hope I will never know.
And this is a wide array of individuals.
I think there's a very troubling belief that homelessness automatically infers bad criminal victimization, all these kind of things.

And I've had the opportunity to speak with people in the downtown who are experiencing homeless who are simply people who are in a position in their life where that seems like the best option for them or the only option for them.

I spoke to an uncle and an niece who have chosen to live within their cycle of addiction chose to live on the streets of downtown because there's a new baby in their house and they don't want to expose the baby to a life of addiction and so they've chosen to live on the streets.
They're coherent, they're conversational, they're real people experiencing real life challenges and they are not the criminal element that the police would normally deal with.

Also a woman wandering in the streets of downtown yelling agitated irrational and when I asked our bike unit hey can you watch out for this woman please like she's she's going to cause a struggle immediately they knew her by name.
They knew where she sleeps they knew a little bit about her.
Challenges with mental health and they said remarkably today she's actually doing really really well.
And that was really impactful on me because it drove home the fact that within the realm of community safety there is so much perspective that we need to have and so much.

You know variants in approach but I'd like to just close with I think one of the biggest challenges in Saskatoon right now from a policing perspective is the number of people who simply came to Saskatoon because they need help or they were residents of Saskatoon who are in a circumstance where they need help and.
It's going to take an entire cohesive collaborative partnership from all sectors and all all people to really make a significant impact.
In so many ways policing is simply keeping a lid on or addressing kind of the visible manifestations of some very very deep and complex issues and needs.
And so how are we going to come together to address those needs that's the question that's that's the big question in our community and who's responsible for which pieces.
So with that maybe I've opened the door to a lot of things but I'm certainly an open book and welcome any questions you may have for me within the realm of policing and Saskatoon safety in general.

It is potentially a significant benefit really and I would welcome the opportunity to have additional conversations as to how we can make that.
Grow and have access to more.
Particularly as the city grows having the ability to utilize cameras.
You know some jurisdictions are utilizing drone programs as kind of their technology answer to cameras but regardless.
Wouldn't it be amazing if we had a camera on every bridge in South Patuna so that somebody in crisis who's calling in their lowest moment saying they're on the bridge can be.
Can be seen immediately and enable us to go directly to them without wasting time knowing where they are what you know what what they're experiencing I think it's amazing.

Well that's something I'll talk offline and even with downtown what I see to just get those conversations happening because I think it's minimal investment that we can maybe work as a city and partner with them on and I'd like to have a camera on every block downtown right now in every bridge that we have downtown.
So I'm glad to hear that you're open to that conversation that's great to hear last but not least I just want to make the comment that.
